stimulus.text:
“To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them. The fifteen thousand tenant houses that were the despair of the sanitarian in the past generation have swelled into thirty-seven thousand, and more than twelve hundred thousand persons call them home.”

Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890), Introduction.
stimulus.source_note: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain; text checked against Project Gutenberg eBook 45502.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stem: According to Riis, what share of New York’s people lived in the tenements?

options.misconception: Guesses a half instead of reading the fraction.
Guesses a tenth instead of reading the fraction.

rationales.A: Riis writes that “three-fourths of its people live in the tenements.”
rationales.B: One-fourth is the opposite share. Riis says three-fourths.
rationales.C: One-half is too small. Riis says three-fourths.
rationales.D: One-tenth is far too small. Riis says three-fourths.
rationales.general:
Find the fraction in the first sentence.
1. Riis says three-fourths of the city’s people live in the tenements.
2. Three-fourths means three out of every four people.
3. That is most of the city, not a small part.
4. The other fractions in the options do not match the text.
Remember: when a passage gives you a number, use that number.
